name: F-2
tagline: Japan's F-16-derived multirole fighter, built for maritime strike. Larger and more composite-intensive than the F-16 it is based on, with an indigenously developed AESA radar, it was purpose-built for anti-ship and air-defense missions around the Japanese home islands.
history: The F-2 traces back to Japan's late-1980s plan to develop a successor to its aging F-1 support fighters, initially as a purely domestic design. Diplomatic pressure from Washington, sharpened by trade tensions including the Toshiba-Kongsberg technology-transfer scandal, pushed Japan into a bilateral program instead: a November 1988 memorandum brought General Dynamics (later Lockheed Martin) in as a partner, contributing F-16 technology and up to 45 percent of development work, with program costs split roughly 60/40 between Japan and the United States. The resulting aircraft, though visibly related to the F-16, was extensively reworked - more than 95 percent of the F-16's engineering drawings were changed, with a 25-percent-larger wing built from co-cured graphite-epoxy composite (a first for a tactical fighter), a longer fuselage, wider nose, three-piece bird-strike-resistant canopy and ten weapons stations against the F-16's six. It was also the first operational fighter in the world to fly with an AESA radar, Japan's indigenously developed J/APG-1. The prototype first flew on 7 October 1995, but structural problems discovered during testing delayed service entry to 2000, and cost growth - the unit price ran to roughly four times that of a contemporary Block 50/52 F-16 - led Japan to cut its planned buy from 141 aircraft to 98, including four prototypes, before production ended in 2011. In service, the F-2 has flown air-defense scramble missions against Russian and Chinese aircraft approaching Japanese airspace and forms a core part of Japan's anti-ship strike capability. The type suffered a serious blow in the March 2011 Tohoku earthquake and tsunami, when floodwater damaged 18 F-2Bs at Matsushima Air Base, five of which were subsequently written off. With production over and the airframe aging, Japan is now developing its successor through the trilateral Global Combat Air Programme (GCAP) with the United Kingdom and Italy, targeting a combat debut around 2035.

flightradar24.howToFind: F-2s rarely broadcast civil ADS-B during operational sorties, so Flightradar24 sightings are limited; occasional appearances come from training and transit flights near JASDF bases such as Misawa, Tsuiki and Matsushima, or at Japanese air show events like the Misawa or Nyutabaru air festivals.

quickFacts: The F-2 beat the F-22 to a milestone: its J/APG-1 was the world's first active electronically scanned array (AESA) radar on a production fighter, in 2000.
It looks like an F-16 but is 25% larger in wing area, built with a co-cured composite wing that US industry later borrowed back.
The 2011 tsunami submerged 18 F-2Bs at Matsushima air base - 13 were rebuilt in a salvage program that cost more than new jets.
Japanese crews nicknamed it the 'Viper Zero' - an F-16 'Viper' descendant built by the maker of the wartime Zero.
Its successor is being designed with Britain and Italy under GCAP - Japan's first fighter partnership beyond the US.

overview: The Mitsubishi F-2 is a Japanese single-engine multirole fighter developed jointly by Mitsubishi Heavy Industries and Lockheed Martin, based on an enlarged F-16 airframe. It was the first production fighter fitted with an active electronically scanned array (AESA) radar.{{ref:wiki-f2}}

Ninety-eight were built for the Japan Air Self-Defense Force at roughly four times the cost of an F-16, reflecting the price of the 1980s trade dispute that killed Japan's original indigenous design.{{ref:wiki-fsx}} It is due to be replaced by the GCAP fighter from 2035.

sections.heading: Origins & Concept
paragraphs: The FS-X program of the mid-1980s began as Japanese autonomy: Mitsubishi's engineers wanted a clean-sheet successor to their F-1 strike fighter. Washington - mid-trade-war, alarmed at Japanese techno-nationalism - pressed hard, and the 1987 compromise made history's most argued-over fighter deal: Japan would co-develop a heavily modified F-16 with General Dynamics, sharing (and paying for) the result.{{ref:wiki-fsx}}

Congress fought the deal, Tokyo resented it, and the engineering proceeded anyway: a 25% larger co-cured composite wing, longer fuselage, bigger nose for a Japanese radar, drag chute, and strengthening for the quartet of heavyweight ASM-1/ASM-2 anti-ship missiles that defined the mission - defending the sea lanes of an island nation.{{ref:wiki-f2}}

sections.heading: Design & Engineering
paragraphs: The F-2's superlatives hide in its skin and nose: the wing was among the first co-cured composite structures on any fighter (technology American industry gained from the program - the sharing ran both ways), and the J/APG-1 made it the first production fighter in the world with an AESA radar, entering service in 2000 while Western equivalents were still in test.{{ref:wiki-f2}}

Mission shaped everything else: the big wing carries four 600+ kg sea-skimming missiles plus tanks and Sidewinders on maritime strike profiles no baseline F-16 could fly, and later upgrades added JDAM precision strike and the improved J/APG-2 with AAM-4B - keeping the 'Viper Zero' (its nickname honouring Mitsubishi's other famous fighter) current through mid-life.{{ref:wiki-f2}}

sections.heading: Service History
paragraphs: Ninety-eight F-2s (of 141 once planned - cost cut the rest) have flown the Japan Air Self-Defense Force's hardest geography since 2000: anti-ship strike squadrons facing the sea approaches, and a share of the relentless scramble mission against Russian and Chinese probes that makes the JASDF one of the world's busiest intercept forces. Like all JSDF equipment, its combat record is, by constitutional design, empty; its value has instead been measured by decades of readiness.{{ref:wiki-f2}}

Its cruellest day came from the sea it guards: the 2011 Tōhoku tsunami drowned 18 F-2Bs of the training wing at Matsushima - nearly a fifth of the fleet - in one afternoon. Japan's response was characteristic: 13 were painstakingly rebuilt over years at costs no accountant loved, because 98 airframes minus 18 was a strategic hole, not a line item.{{ref:wiki-f2}}

sections.heading: Development
paragraphs: The F-2's ledger reads both ways. Against it: unit costs near four times an F-16's, a truncated buy, and early wing-crack and radar teething that critics feasted on. For it: technologies (AESA, co-cured composites) that led the world, an industrial base kept alive, and a fighter precisely fitted to a mission imported types weren't.{{ref:wiki-fsx}}

Its succession is the lesson applied: after the F-2's dependence experience, Japan launched its F-X/next-fighter effort determined to hold design authority - merging it in 2022 with Britain and Italy as GCAP{{ref:tdn-gcap}}, the sixth-generation programme whose 2035 planned service entry is timed to the F-2's retirement.{{ref:wiki-gcap}}

sections.heading: Current Status & Outlook
paragraphs: The F-2 is the bridge between Japan's licence-building past and design-authority future: the program that transferred enough capability - painfully, expensively - for Mitsubishi's engineers to demonstrate X-2 stealth technology and negotiate GCAP as equals. Nations remember their tuition; the F-2 was Japan's.{{ref:wiki-fsx}}
As an aircraft it retires with a strong reputation: an early AESA-radar pioneer, and the fighter that spent 35 years guarding Japan's sea lanes without ever firing in anger.{{ref:wiki-f2}}

accidentsAndIncidents.title: Crash on takeoff at Nagoya after maintenance
accidentsAndIncidents.summary: An F-2B being test-flown after maintenance crashed during takeoff at Nagoya (Komaki) Airfield. Both test pilots survived with minor injuries; the investigation attributed the crash to improper wiring work.

accidentsAndIncidents.title: Fleet wrecked by the Tōhoku tsunami
accidentsAndIncidents.summary: The 2011 Tōhoku earthquake and tsunami flooded Matsushima Air Base, damaging or destroying 18 F-2Bs on the ground. Five were scrapped as beyond repair; the remaining 13 were repaired over several years at a cost of roughly ¥80 billion.

accidentsAndIncidents.title: Training crash into the Sea of Japan
accidentsAndIncidents.summary: An F-2B crashed into the Sea of Japan during a training flight. Both the instructor and pilot ejected and survived.

accidentsAndIncidents.title: Crash off Ibaraki grounds the F-2A fleet
accidentsAndIncidents.summary: An F-2A from Hyakuri Air Base crashed into the Pacific Ocean during a training flight off Ibaraki Prefecture. The pilot ejected and was rescued, and Japan grounded its F-2A fleet pending investigation.
